I am a computational plasma physicist at West Virginia University, where I am
currently a visiting researcher and will join the faculty as an assistant
professor in January 2027. My group works at the intersection of applied
mathematics, high-performance computing, and plasma physics. We ask where our
ability to simulate plasmas falls short, and build the numerical methods and
software, including the open-source [Gkeyll](https://github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll)
framework, that make new regimes accessible to modeling. We use these tools to
understand how the smallest scales of a plasma, where individual particle
motions give rise to collective behavior, shape the large-scale evolution of
systems as different as the Sun, accretion disks around black holes, and the
interior of fusion reactors, and we develop theories and predictions for these
systems together with observers and experimentalists. We also bring formal
verification from theoretical computer science to machine learning, building
[provably correct neural networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14853) and
certifiably correct code, so that artificial intelligence can accelerate plasma
physics in ways we can trust.
